questions.enonce_markdown:
Show that the expression $x^2 + 2x + 6$ is positive for all real values of $x$.

Hence, find the set of values of $x$ for which $\dfrac{x}{x-2} > \dfrac{3}{x+5}$. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Positivity.** Complete the square:

$$x^2 + 2x + 6 = (x + 1)^2 + 5.$$

Since $(x+1)^2 \ge 0$ for every real $x$, $(x+1)^2 + 5 \ge 5 > 0$. So $x^2 + 2x + 6 > 0$ for all real $x$. (Alternatively, the discriminant is $4 - 24 = -20 < 0$ and the leading coefficient is positive, so the parabola never meets the $x$-axis and lies above it.) $\blacksquare$

**The inequality.** Do not multiply by $(x-2)(x+5)$ directly, because its sign is not known. Bring everything to one side (with $x \ne 2$ and $x \ne -5$):

$$\frac{x}{x-2} - \frac{3}{x+5} > 0 \Longleftrightarrow \frac{x(x+5) - 3(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+5)} > 0 \Longleftrightarrow \frac{x^2 + 5x - 3x + 6}{(x-2)(x+5)} > 0 \Longleftrightarrow \frac{x^2 + 2x + 6}{(x-2)(x+5)} > 0.$$

By the first part the numerator is always positive, so the fraction is positive exactly when the denominator is positive:

$$(x - 2)(x + 5) > 0.$$

The critical values are $x = -5$ and $x = 2$. The product of the two factors is positive when both factors have the same sign: both positive ($x > 2$) or both negative ($x < -5$).

$$\boxed{\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x < -5 \ \text{or}\ x > 2\}}$$

Check: $x = 3$: $\dfrac{3}{1} = 3 > \dfrac{3}{8}$ (true); $x = -6$: $\dfrac{-6}{-8} = 0.75 > \dfrac{3}{-1} = -3$ (true); $x = 0$: $0 > \dfrac35$ (false); $x = -3$: $\dfrac{-3}{-5} = 0.6 > \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5$ (false).

questions.enonce_markdown: Three cards are to be drawn from a pack of 52 playing cards. In how many ways can this be done if the cards must consist of 2 clubs and 1 diamond? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A pack contains $13$ cards of each suit. Choose the $2$ clubs from the $13$ clubs and the $1$ diamond from the $13$ diamonds; the choices are independent, so multiply:

$$\binom{13}{2}\times\binom{13}{1} = 78 \times 13 = 1014.$$

$$\boxed{1014 \text{ ways}}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Three cards are to be drawn from a pack of 52 playing cards. In how many ways can this be done if two or more cards must not come from the same suit? (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The condition says that no two of the three cards may come from the same suit, so the three cards must come from three different suits.

**Choose the suits.** Three of the four suits can be chosen in $\dbinom{4}{3} = 4$ ways.

**Choose one card from each of these suits.** Each suit has $13$ cards, so there are $13 \times 13 \times 13 = 2197$ ways.

$$4 \times 13^3 = 4 \times 2197 = 8788.$$

$$\boxed{8788 \text{ ways}}$$

Check by complement: the total number of 3-card hands is $\dbinom{52}{3} = 22100$. Hands with at least two cards from the same suit: all three of one suit, $4\binom{13}{3} = 1144$, plus exactly two of one suit and the third from another suit, $4\binom{13}{2}\times 39 = 12168$; total $13312$. Then $22100 - 13312 = 8788$. Correct.
